common_name: Buckley's Quill Mock Orange (Ottawa-Bred Quill-Petaled Double Mock Orange)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; this Ottawa Research Station selection is exceptionally cold-hardy for a mock orange, so it suits colder gardens than most Lemoine hybrids.

directions: Bred at Agricultural Canada's Ottawa Research Station from a 1959 cross and selected in 1961, Buckley's Quill carries an unusual double flower with roughly 30 narrow, pointed petals that give the fragrant white blooms a distinctive quilled look unlike any other mock orange. Dense clusters open along an erect, compact frame in late spring to early summer, drawing heavy bee activity, above pubescent yellow-green foliage that adds mild textural interest even out of bloom. Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun for the heaviest flowering, though it tolerates part shade. Prune right after flowering, removing a portion of the oldest canes at the base each year to keep new wood producing strongly.

common_name: Sybille Mock Orange (Purple-Centered Compact Mock Orange)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Sybille stays smaller and wider than most purpureomaculatus-group mock oranges, so give it room to arch outward rather than upward.

directions: Sybille belongs to Victor Lemoine's purpureomaculatus breeding line and later served as a parent of the popular cultivar Beauclerk, passing on its signature trait: creamy-white, cup-shaped flowers stained deeply with purple at the center. Bloom is profuse through early to midsummer on a low, wide, arching frame that spreads noticeably farther than it grows tall, making it useful as a spilling accent along a border edge or low wall. The fragrance is sweet and pronounced, carrying well on warm evenings. Grow in average, well-drained soil in full sun, and prune immediately after flowering since next year's blooms form on the current season's wood.
sources: Hillier Manual of Trees and Shrubs

common_name: Silver Showers Mock Orange (Compact Lemoinei Fragrant Mock Orange)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Silver Showers grows quickly and can live for decades, so choose a permanent spot with at least 6 hours of direct sun for best bloom.

directions: This German-raised member of the lemoinei group forms a shapely, multi-stemmed shrub with gracefully arching branches and narrow, pointed, dark green leaves that are smooth above and softly hairy beneath. Fragrant white flowers up to 1.5 inches across open in terminal racemes of three to seven blooms in late spring to early summer, giving a fuller floral display than many single-flowered mock oranges of similar size. It grows at a notably fast rate for the genus and can remain a garden fixture for roughly 30 years with only routine care. Site in full sun in average, well-drained soil and prune right after flowering to avoid removing next year's buds.

common_name: Frosty Morn Mock Orange (Compact Double-Flowered Fragrant Mock Orange)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light dappled shade; Frosty Morn's tidy rounded habit reaches full size over about 7 to 10 years, making it a good scaled choice for smaller borders and containers.

directions: Frosty Morn is a compact hybrid mock orange notable for fully double, pure white flowers gathered into tight, fragrant bouquets that open from early summer against dark green, toothed, ovate foliage. Its rounded, dense habit stays considerably smaller than most mock orange cultivars, reaching a mature size measured in feet rather than the sprawling scale typical of the genus, so it fits small gardens and mixed borders without overwhelming neighboring plants. It was later used as a parent in breeding the quill-petaled cultivar Buckley's Quill, passing along its heavy double flowering. Grow in fertile, well-drained soil in sun or light shade, and prune lightly right after bloom to maintain its neat form.

common_name: Candidissima Deutzia (Tall Double White-Flowered Fuzzy Deutzia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Candidissima grows considerably taller than the wild species, so allow extra vertical room against a fence or backdrop planting.

directions: Candidissima is a robust, RHS Award of Garden Merit selection of the fuzzy deutzia that produces large, dense clusters of fully double, pure white, honey-scented flowers through June and July, well after most spring shrubs have finished blooming. It grows notably taller and more vigorous than the species itself, developing slightly drooping branch tips at maturity that give older plants a graceful, fountain-like outline. The felted, rough-textured leaves typical of Deutzia scabra persist through the season as a coarse-textured backdrop for the flower clusters. Grow in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, and thin out a share of the oldest wood at ground level each year after flowering to keep the shrub renewing vigorously.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; the gracefully arching canes of Contraste look best given open space to cascade rather than being crowded by neighboring shrubs.

directions: Contraste is part of the influential group of hybrid deutzias raised by Victor Lemoine and introduced between 1925 and 1936, prized for star-shaped flowers similar in soft pink tone to the well-known cultivar Mont Rose but marked with a noticeably darker stripe running down the reverse of each petal. This RHS Award of Garden Merit shrub carries its early-summer flower clusters along gracefully arching branches, giving a softer, more cascading profile than upright deutzia cultivars. Foliage is a clean mid-green through the growing season, providing a plain backdrop that lets the bicolor flowers stand out. Grow in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, and renew the shrub each year after bloom by removing some of the oldest flowering canes at the base.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; the semi-weeping branches of this hybrid look best sited where they can cascade over a low wall or slope rather than being staked upright.

directions: Introduced around 1900 by Victor Lemoine from a cross of Deutzia parviflora and Deutzia purpurascens, this hybrid produces upright clusters of star-shaped flowers that open white with a broad, darker pink stripe running down the back of each petal, a bicolor effect most visible before the buds fully open. Its branches take on a distinctive semi-weeping arch as the shrub matures, giving it a softer silhouette than most upright deutzias, and the oblong, finely toothed leaves often flush purple in autumn for a secondary season of interest. It tolerates acidic, neutral, or alkaline soils as long as drainage is reasonable. Grow in full sun to partial shade, and prune out a portion of old flowering wood right after bloom to keep new growth vigorous.

common_name: Fasciculata Deutzia (Clustered Pale Pink-Flowered Elegantissima Deutzia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in fertile, neutral to alkaline, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; pinch young stem tips to encourage a bushier, denser habit before the shrub reaches its full 5 to 10 year maturity.

directions: Fasciculata is an upright cultivar of the elegantissima hybrid group, forming dense, clustered heads of five-petaled, pale rose-pink flowers that open from noticeably darker pink buds in late spring to early summer against oval, toothed leaves. Its habit runs taller and more columnar than many other elegantissima selections, making it a fitting choice for a narrow border spot or as a backdrop shrub rather than a groundcover role. The shrub reaches full size over roughly five to ten years and responds well to renewal pruning. Grow in fertile, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun to partial shade, and cut flowering stems back hard immediately after bloom to encourage strong new wood for the following season.
